JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- Ten South African ministers and the deputy president have resigned as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to leave office. South African President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation in a televised address Sunday. His replacement, African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe, will be sworn in as South Africa's president Thursday. Mbeki announced he was resigning on Sunday, prompting threats from several Cabinet members to follow suit -- but the outgoing president urged them to stay in office, government sources said. The resignations, which include Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, will take effect Thursday when Mbeki steps down, a government statement said. "All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement said. The finance minister's assistant told CNN that Manuel is willing to serve in the new government, if needed. Three deputy ministers have also tendered their resignations, a government statement said. A spokesman for South Africa's ruling party, the African National Congress, confirmed that it has named Motlanthe as its choice to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe will stay in office until elections in the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win. Earlier this month, the ANC asked Mbeki to step down after a judge threw out the corruption, fraud and racketeering case against Zuma -- Mbeki's political arch rival. The judge called the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference. Mbeki -- who has been South Africa's president for nearly 10 years -- spoke of some of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation on Sunday during a televised address.  Watch the significance of Mbeki "falling on the sword" » . "I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said. Under his leadership the country has had the longest period of sustained economic growth in the South Africa's history and has reached out to indigent people in an unprecedented way, Mbeki said. Mbeki said the country still has economic, corruption and crime challenges to face in the future. And he gave his vote of confidence to the country's next leader without naming who that leader would be. Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced Saturday that the party -- which Mbeki has been involved with since his teens -- had asked him to leave before his term was up. Mbeki agreed to do so, he said. Mantashe said the ANC made the decision "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country" and so the ANC movement could remain "stable and unified." The case against Zuma -- who replaced Mbeki as ANC president last year -- was thrown out in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority recharged him. Judge Chris Nicholson made no ruling on Zuma's guilt or innocence, and he could be recharged. Political observers doubted that would happen because of Zuma's popularity, particularly with the Communist Party and trade unions. Zuma has denied the charges. He said the case was politically motivated, and harmed his chances to become the ANC's presidential nominee. He could have faced at least 15 years in jail if convicted of accepting bribes from a company that got a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal. He also faced charges of having a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes for Zuma and using Zuma's political influence to benefit his businesses. Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics alleged he pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma. Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing deal between Zimbabwe's political rivals, who signed the agreement on Monday in an effort to put aside the violent past and end the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March. Under it, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, has become prime minister and the coordinator of government affairs.

outputs.L1:
JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- Ten South African ministers, along with the deputy president, have tendered their resignations as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to depart from office. Mbeki announced his resignation in a televised address on Sunday. His successor, African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe, is scheduled to be sworn in as South Africa's president on Thursday.

Following Mbeki's resignation announcement on Sunday, several Cabinet members threatened to follow suit; however, government sources indicate that the outgoing president urged them to remain in their posts. According to a government statement, the resignations—including those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota—will take effect Thursday, coinciding with Mbeki's departure.

"All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement noted. The finance minister's assistant informed CNN that Manuel remains willing to serve in the new government, should his services be required. Additionally, three deputy ministers have submitted their resignations, according to a government statement.

A spokesman for South Africa's ruling party, the African National Congress, confirmed that Motlanthe has been designated as the party's choice to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe will serve until the elections scheduled for next spring, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win.

Earlier this month, the ANC called upon Mbeki to step down after a judge dismissed the corruption, fraud, and racketeering case against Zuma—Mbeki's longtime political rival. The judge deemed the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference.

Mbeki, who has led South Africa for nearly a decade, reflected on several of his achievements during his formal resignation address on Sunday. "I depart this office knowing that many men and women in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki stated. He noted that under his leadership, the country experienced its longest period of sustained economic growth in South African history, alongside unprecedented outreach efforts to assist the nation's most impoverished citizens. Mbeki acknowledged that the country continues to face challenges related to the economy, corruption, and crime, and expressed his confidence in the nation's next leader, though he did not name that individual.

Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced Saturday that the party—with which Mbeki has been affiliated since his teenage years—had requested he step down before the conclusion of his term. Mbeki agreed to comply. Mantashe explained that the ANC made this decision "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country," and to ensure that the ANC movement itself remained "stable and unified."

The case against Zuma, who succeeded Mbeki as ANC president last year, was initially dismissed in September 2006, though the National Prosecuting Authority subsequently recharged him. Judge Chris Nicholson issued no ruling regarding Zuma's guilt or innocence, leaving open the possibility that charges could be reinstated. However, political observers considered this unlikely, given Zuma's substantial popularity—particularly among the Communist Party and trade unions.

Zuma has consistently denied the charges against him, asserting that the case was politically motivated and detrimental to his prospects of becoming the ANC's presidential nominee. Had he been convicted of accepting bribes from a company awarded a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal, he could have faced a minimum of 15 years in prison. He also faced allegations of maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is currently serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf and leveraging Zuma's political influence to benefit his own business interests.

Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics have alleged that he was instrumental in pursuing the corruption charges against Zuma.

Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe's rival political factions, who signed the accord on Monday in an effort to move beyond a turbulent past and resolve the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since the disputed national elections in March. Under the terms of this agreement, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his longstanding rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, assumes the role of prime minister and coordinator of government affairs.

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- Amid President Thabo Mbeki's departure from office, a group of ten South African cabinet ministers along with the deputy president have stepped down from their positions. In a Sunday evening broadcast, Mbeki confirmed he would be stepping down from the presidency. Taking his place will be Kgalema Motlanthe, currently serving as deputy president of the African National Congress, who is scheduled to be inaugurated as the nation's leader on Thursday.

Following Mbeki's Sunday resignation announcement, multiple Cabinet officials indicated they might also quit their posts. However, according to government insiders, Mbeki encouraged them to remain in their positions. A government statement confirmed that the resignations—which include those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota—would become official on Thursday, coinciding with Mbeki's departure.

The statement noted, "All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them." According to Manuel's assistant, who spoke with CNN, the finance minister remains open to continuing his role under the new leadership if his services are needed. Additionally, a government statement revealed that three deputy ministers submitted resignation letters as well.

An ANC spokesperson verified that the party had selected Motlanthe as Mbeki's successor. He will hold the presidency until next spring's elections, in which ANC President Jacob Zuma is expected by most observers to emerge victorious.

Earlier in the month, the ANC pushed for Mbeki's resignation following a judge's dismissal of corruption, fraud, and racketeering charges against Zuma, who has long been Mbeki's political adversary. The presiding judge deemed the prosecution improper and suggested that Mbeki's administration had politically manipulated the proceedings.

During his nearly decade-long tenure as South Africa's president, Mbeki used his formal resignation speech on Sunday to reflect on his accomplishments. "I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," he stated. He pointed to the country's longest stretch of continuous economic expansion under his governance, along with unprecedented efforts to assist impoverished citizens. Mbeki acknowledged that South Africa continues to grapple with issues surrounding its economy, corruption, and crime rates. Without specifically identifying his successor, he expressed confidence in the nation's future leadership.

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe disclosed that the party—which Mbeki joined as a young man—had requested his early departure from office, a request he ultimately honored. Mantashe explained that this decision was made "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country" and to preserve unity and stability within the ANC movement itself.

The legal proceedings against Zuma, who succeeded Mbeki as ANC president the previous year, were initially dismissed in September 2006, though the National Prosecuting Authority subsequently refiled charges. Judge Chris Nicholson's ruling did not address Zuma's guilt or innocence, leaving open the possibility of future prosecution. However, political analysts considered this unlikely given Zuma's substantial support base, especially among trade unions and the Communist Party. Zuma has consistently maintained his innocence, characterizing the prosecution as politically driven and damaging to his presidential aspirations within the ANC. Had he been convicted of bribery charges connected to a company's involvement in a massive arms deal, he could have received a prison sentence of 15 years or more. Separate allegations concerned an improper financial relationship with his onetime adviser Schabir Shaik, who is currently serving a 15-year term for bribery solicitation on Zuma's behalf and for exploiting Zuma's political connections for personal business gain.

At 66 years old, Mbeki took over the presidency from Nelson Mandela in June 1999. Some critics have accused him of orchestrating the corruption case against Zuma. In other diplomatic efforts, Mbeki recently facilitated a power-sharing arrangement between rival factions in Zimbabwe, who formalized the agreement this past Monday in a bid to move past the country's turbulent history and resolve the ongoing crisis triggered by the contested March elections. Under the terms of this deal, Robert Mugabe continues as Zimbabwe's president, while his longstanding political opponent, Morgan Tsvangirai, assumes the role of prime minister overseeing government operations.

# South African Political Transition: Mass Resignations Follow Mbeki's Departure

South Africa was thrust into a period of significant political transition this week as ten government ministers and the deputy president tendered their resignations in the wake of President Thabo Mbeki's televised address announcing his own departure from office. The wave of resignations underscores the depth of the political upheaval that has gripped the ruling African National Congress (ANC) and the broader government structure.

## Motlanthe to Assume Presidency

African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe is set to be sworn in as South Africa's new head of state on Thursday. Notably, this date coincides with the day on which the resignations of the ministers and the deputy president officially take effect, creating a coordinated handover of power designed to facilitate a smoother transition despite the circumstances surrounding it.

## Calls for Continuity Amid Upheaval

Despite the political turmoil, Mbeki has urged members of his Cabinet to remain in their current positions rather than step down alongside him. In response, those ministers who chose to resign have nonetheless expressed their willingness to support the transition process, offering their assistance to ensure the incoming administration under Motlanthe can establish itself effectively during this delicate period.

## Origins of the Political Crisis

The current situation traces back to earlier this month, when the ANC formally requested that Mbeki step down from the presidency. This demand followed a significant legal development in which a judge dismissed corruption charges that had been brought against Jacob Zuma, the president of the ANC. In dismissing the case, the judge went further, accusing Mbeki's government of having politically interfered in the judicial proceedings against Zuma—a charge that proved politically damaging enough to precipitate Mbeki's resignation.

## Looking Ahead to Elections

Motlanthe's tenure as president is expected to be a transitional one, lasting only until spring elections scheduled for next year. Political observers widely anticipate that Jacob Zuma, in his capacity as ANC President, will emerge victorious in that electoral contest, positioning him to assume the presidency in his own right once the party's traditional path to power following electoral success plays out. This expectation adds a layer of significance to Motlanthe's caretaker role, as it is widely viewed as a bridge to Zuma's anticipated ascension to the nation's highest office.

South Africa was thrust into political turmoil this week following the resignation of President Thabo Mbeki, a move that triggered a cascade of departures within his government. In the wake of Mbeki's announcement, ten government ministers, along with Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and three deputy ministers, also submitted their resignations. Despite stepping down, these officials have agreed to remain in their positions temporarily to assist with a smooth transition of power, ensuring that government functions are not disrupted during this critical period.

In a significant development, Kgalema Motlanthe, a senior figure within the ruling African National Congress (ANC), has been named to succeed Mbeki as president. Motlanthe is scheduled to be formally sworn in as South Africa's new head of state on Thursday, marking a swift transfer of leadership amid the political upheaval.

The roots of this crisis trace back to a court ruling in which a judge dismissed corruption charges that had been brought against Jacob Zuma, Mbeki's long-standing political rival within the ANC. In delivering the ruling, the judge went further, sharply criticizing what was characterized as improper government interference in the judicial process—allegations that implicated Mbeki's administration in attempting to manipulate the case against Zuma for political purposes.

This judicial rebuke proved to be a turning point, galvanizing support within the ANC to force Mbeki from office. Party leaders, increasingly aligned with Zuma and troubled by the implications of the court's findings, moved decisively to push Mbeki out of the presidency, effectively ending his tenure before the natural conclusion of his term.

Under the current arrangement, Motlanthe will serve as a caretaker president, holding the office until national elections are held next spring. Political observers widely anticipate that Zuma, now cleared of the corruption charges that had threatened to derail his political career, will emerge victorious in that electoral contest, positioning him to become South Africa's next full-term president and cementing his political rehabilitation following the contentious legal battle.

# Johannesburg: The Heartbeat of South Africa

Johannesburg, often affectionately called "Jozi" or "Egoli" (City of Gold), stands as South Africa's largest city and its undisputed economic powerhouse. Unlike Cape Town or Pretoria, Johannesburg was not founded for political or strategic reasons but emerged from the discovery of gold in 1886, transforming a quiet stretch of highveld into one of the fastest-growing cities in history.

## A City Born from Gold

The discovery of the Witwatersrand gold reef sparked a rush that drew fortune-seekers from across the globe. Within just a few years, a sprawling mining camp evolved into a bustling metropolis. This rapid, unplanned growth shaped much of Johannesburg's character—a city built on ambition, hustle, and reinvention.

## A Complex History

Johannesburg's history is deeply intertwined with South Africa's broader story, including the painful legacy of apartheid. Soweto, a township on the city's outskirts, became a symbol of resistance during the anti-apartheid struggle, most notably during the 1976 uprising. Today, sites like the Apartheid Museum and Constitution Hill offer visitors profound insight into this history and the nation's journey toward democracy.

## Economic and Cultural Hub

As the financial capital of South Africa, Johannesburg hosts the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the largest on the African continent. The city is home to numerous multinational corporations, a thriving arts scene, and diverse neighborhoods reflecting the many cultures that make up modern South Africa. Areas like Maboneng and Braamfontein showcase urban renewal through street art, galleries, and vibrant nightlife.

## Gateway to Adventure

Beyond its urban energy, Johannesburg serves as a gateway to South Africa's natural wonders. Visitors often use the city as a starting point for safaris to Kruger National Park or trips to the scenic Drakensberg mountains.

## Conclusion

Johannesburg embodies the resilience and diversity of South Africa itself—a city that has risen from its complicated past to become a dynamic symbol of African enterprise, culture, and hope for the future.

# South African Cabinet Resigns En Masse Following Mbeki's Departure

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa** — In a dramatic political upheaval, several senior members of South Africa's Cabinet tendered their resignations this week, following the resignation of President Thabo Mbeki, deepening a political crisis within the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

Mbeki stepped down on September 21, 2008, after the ANC's national executive committee formally requested his departure. The move came after a judge's ruling suggested Mbeki may have improperly interfered in corruption charges against his rival, Jacob Zuma — allegations Mbeki has denied.

In the wake of Mbeki's resignation, at least 10 Cabinet ministers and deputy ministers announced they would also be stepping down, in what analysts describe as a show of loyalty to the departing president and a signal of the deep factional rift within the ANC.

Among those who resigned were Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, a figure widely credited with steering South Africa's economy through years of steady growth, and Foreign Minister Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma. Manuel's departure in particular rattled financial markets, given his reputation for fiscal discipline and his long tenure managing the treasury.

"This is about more than personal loyalty — it reflects real anxiety about the direction of economic policy and governance," said one Johannesburg-based political analyst. "Manuel's resignation sent a shockwave through investors."

Kgalema Motlanthe, the ANC's deputy president, was sworn in as interim president to lead the country until national elections scheduled for 2009. Motlanthe, seen as a unifying figure within the fractured party, quickly moved to accept some resignations while urging other ministers to remain in their posts "in the interest of stability and continuity of government."

The political turmoil stems from a long-simmering rivalry between Mbeki and Zuma, who was elected ANC president in December 2007 despite facing corruption charges related to a multibillion-dollar arms deal. Zuma's supporters have accused Mbeki's administration of using state institutions to undermine Zuma's political ambitions.

The judge's ruling last week, which was later set aside on appeal, had raised the explosive suggestion of political meddling in the National Prosecuting Authority, intensifying calls from Zuma allies for Mbeki to step down immediately.

Financial markets reacted nervously to the news, with the South African rand weakening against major currencies amid uncertainty over the country's economic policy direction. The Johannesburg Stock Exchange saw volatile trading as investors weighed the implications of the reshuffle.

International reaction has been largely cautious, with several governments and organizations expressing hope that South Africa's democratic institutions would ensure a smooth transition. The African Union and the Southern African Development Community both issued statements urging unity and adherence to constitutional processes.

Mbeki, who served nearly a decade as president after succeeding Nelson Mandela in 1999, leaves behind a mixed legacy — credited with fostering economic growth and a more assertive African foreign policy, but criticized for his government's slow response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic and allegations of political interference.

As South Africa braces for further political realignment ahead of the 2009 elections, all eyes remain on Zuma, who is expected to become the ANC's candidate for the presidency despite the corruption charges still looming over him.

Motlanthe is expected to announce a reshuffled Cabinet in the coming days as he seeks to stabilize the government during the transition period.

---

*This story is developing and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

**Background: The Mbeki-Zuma Rivalry**

The crisis stemmed from a bitter power struggle within the African National Congress (ANC) between President Thabo Mbeki and his former deputy, Jacob Zuma. Tensions escalated after Mbeki dismissed Zuma as deputy president in 2005 amid corruption allegations.

**The ANC's Role**

In December 2007, Zuma defeated Mbeki to become president of the ANC itself, giving Zuma control of the party even though Mbeki remained head of state. This created an unusual split in power. Tensions came to a head in September 2008 when a judge suggested there may have been political interference by Mbeki's administration in corruption charges brought against Zuma. Though the corruption case against Zuma was ultimately dropped, the ANC's National Executive Committee decided to formally recall Mbeki, effectively forcing him to step down.

**Mbeki's Resignation**

Facing pressure from the party he had once led, Mbeki announced his resignation as President of South Africa on **September 21, 2008**. He stepped down formally shortly thereafter, ending his presidency before completing his term.

**Succession**

Kgalema Motlanthe, the Deputy President of the ANC, was appointed as **interim President** by Parliament to serve out the remainder of Mbeki's term. However, Jacob Zuma—as leader of the ANC—was widely expected to become President following national elections scheduled for **2009**, given the ANC's dominant electoral position in South African politics.

# South Africa's President Resigns Amid Corruption Case Fallout

**Johannesburg** — President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation on September 21, 2008, following a decision by the African National Congress (ANC) National Executive Committee to recall him from office, marking one of the most significant political crises in post-apartheid South Africa.

## Background to the Recall

The recall came directly in the aftermath of a ruling by Judge Chris Nicholson in the Durban High Court, which addressed corruption charges against Jacob Zuma, the ANC party president. Zuma had faced allegations related to a multi-billion-rand arms deal, with prosecutors accusing him of accepting bribes from arms manufacturer Thint (a subsidiary of the French company Thales).

Judge Nicholson's ruling, while primarily addressing procedural issues in the prosecution of Zuma, included remarks suggesting there may have been political interference in the timing and handling of the case against Zuma. The judge implied that Mbeki's government may have manipulated the prosecutorial process to disadvantage Zuma, his political rival, following a bitter succession battle within the ANC.

## Political Rivalry Context

The Mbeki-Zuma relationship had deteriorated significantly since 2005, when Mbeki dismissed Zuma as Deputy President following corruption allegations linked to his financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who was convicted of soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf. This dismissal set the stage for a fierce leadership contest within the ANC, culminating in Zuma's victory over Mbeki for the party presidency at the ANC's Polokwane conference in December 2007.

## The Recall Decision

Following Judge Nicholson's comments, ANC leadership determined that Mbeki's continued presidency was untenable, citing:

- Erosion of public trust in the impartiality of state institutions
- Concerns about the relationship between the executive and the National Prosecuting Authority
- Pressure to demonstrate party unity ahead of 2009 elections
- The need to distance the ANC from perceptions of using state apparatus for political ends

## Aftermath

Mbeki's resignation led to Kgalema Motlanthe serving as interim president until elections in 2009, which Zuma's ANC won decisively, paving the way for Zuma to become President.

The charges against Zuma were later dropped in April 2009, just weeks before the election, with the National Prosecuting Authority citing procedural irregularities—a decision that remained controversial for years afterward and would resurface in subsequent legal battles.

---

*This event significantly shaped South African politics, highlighting tensions between judicial independence, executive power, and internal party dynamics within the ANC during a critical transitional period.*

# South Africa Turns a Page: Motlanthe Steps In as Mbeki Era Ends

**JOHANNESBURG** — In a moment that has been building for months, South Africa's political landscape shifted dramatically as Kgalema Motlanthe assumed the presidency, marking the end of Thabo Mbeki's tenure and exposing the deep fractures within the African National Congress that have defined the nation's politics for the better part of a decade.

## A Presidency Cut Short

Mbeki's departure did not come through the ballot box but through the machinery of his own party. Following a September ruling by a High Court judge suggesting political interference in corruption charges against ANC president Jacob Zuma, the ANC's National Executive Committee moved to recall Mbeki from office—a stunning rebuke for a man who had led both party and country since Nelson Mandela stepped aside.

The recall capped a bitter rivalry that had simmered since Zuma's dismissal as deputy president in 2005, when Mbeki fired him amid a corruption scandal linked to arms deal kickbacks. What followed was a years-long battle for the soul of the ANC, culminating in Zuma's decisive victory over Mbeki for the party presidency at the Polokwane conference in December 2007.

## The Polokwane Fault Line

That conference exposed rifts that had long been papered over. Mbeki's technocratic, market-friendly governance style—praised internationally for economic stability—had alienated key ANC constituencies: the trade union federation COSATU, the South African Communist Party, and grassroots members who felt the post-apartheid economic gains had bypassed the poor.

Zuma, despite facing his own legal troubles, positioned himself as the champion of the party's populist and left-leaning wing. His victory at Polokwane was less an endorsement of Zuma personally than a rejection of what many saw as Mbeki's aloof, centralized style of leadership—critics called it a "presidency of one."

## Enter Motlanthe

With Zuma unable to assume the presidency immediately—still an MP but not yet positioned to take the national presidency before elections—the ANC turned to Motlanthe, the party's deputy president, as a steadying caretaker.

Motlanthe, a former political prisoner on Robben Island and ex-secretary-general of the ANC, brings a reputation as a unifying, low-key figure—someone respected across the party's factions. His selection reflects the ANC's effort to project stability and continuity even as it manages an unprecedented internal transition.

He inherits a government still reeling from the shock of Mbeki's ouster. Several cabinet ministers loyal to Mbeki resigned in solidarity, including Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, though he later agreed to stay on temporarily to reassure jittery markets.

## The Road Ahead

Motlanthe's presidency is widely understood to be transitional, a bridge to Zuma's expected ascension following national elections next year. Yet the events of recent weeks underscore how thoroughly the balance of power has shifted within the ANC—from the state back to the party, and from Mbeki's technocratic inner circle to a broader, more fractious coalition of interests.

For a nation whose stability has often been measured by the ANC's internal cohesion, the question now is whether this transition marks a resolution of the party's divisions—or merely a new chapter in them.
